Our estimation target is the covariance of run deviations that generalise across item halves. We therefore use run covariance for our empirical estimate, reserving a seed-only interpretation for designs with matching training conditions.

Our item-general estimate can differ from the run variance of a fixed evaluation bank. A run can perform differently on particular items without changing its expected score over an item population. Under our measurement model, that variation enters the item error and doesn't contribute to the cross-half covariance target, although repeated evaluation of a fixed item bank can retain this component and its run variance needn't equal the item-general variance estimated here.

Our analogy with quantitative genetics distinguishes covariance between configurations from residual covariance within them, and it doesn't identify separate additive-genetic and shared-environment components in a model-training experiment. Between-configuration correlation $R_P$ reflects differences in recipe and model size. The within-configuration covariance $\Sig$ instead concerns deviations between replicates. Our plug-in comparison asks whether the first correlation structure predicts the second after we supply the marginal run variances.

units.new_text: We pool $T_c$ and $U_c$ across configurations before taking their ratio. Each individual denominator uses two replicate degrees of freedom and can approach zero or become negative, and averaging individual ratios would give those unstable denominators disproportionate influence. Pooling reduces that problem but doesn't remove the effect of configurations with large covariance contributions.

Recomputing the recipe influences from our cluster linearisation gives participation ratios of 3.08 for margins and 9.02 for accuracy. One recipe contributes 0.520 of the squared margin influence, and removing that recipe moves our estimate by 0.037, the largest change any single recipe produces. A leverage-corrected influence divides each recipe residual by one minus that recipe's share of the denominator sum, and applying that correction raises the share to 0.538 and lowers the two ratios to 2.92 and 8.56. Thus the concentration figure depends on the correction a reader assumes, and these quantities describe influence concentration rather than literal counts of independent clusters for inference. Recomputing the permutation experiment ten times at the record's own 1,000 replicates gives margin coverage between 0.915 and 0.942 with a mean of 0.931. The recorded value of 0.925 sits inside that seed-to-seed spread. That record therefore reads as one draw at a replicate count too coarse to separate these values, and together the ten runs put margin coverage 0.019 below nominal.

The covariance moments are unbiased under their assumptions, while our pooled ratio has a random denominator and its square root introduces a second nonlinear transformation. Neither of those transformations therefore inherits exact unbiasedness. A finite implementation must also specify what happens when a pooled sum is nonpositive. The reported data give finite full-battery estimates, though that observation doesn't establish finite estimates for arbitrary input populations.

units.new_text: Different item identifiers can still refer to items with dependent errors, because shared source passages, duplicate questions, and overlapping content can create cross-half covariance. A fixed finite item bank split without replacement also requires a model for its sampling dependence. Our item-half assignment alone can't verify these conditions.

BoolQ has documented shared passages, and we check them directly through the release's request files that carry each question's passage. The passages of all 3,270 questions match the google/boolq validation split exactly, giving 2,938 passages with 578 questions in passages of two or more. A passage-aware split assigns whole passages to halves and then averages questions. Half sizes therefore differ by a few items and the equal-half derivation doesn't hold exactly. On one such split the margin and accuracy estimates are 1.248 and 1.097 against 1.244 and 1.078 on the frozen split. Across fifty paired re-splits the passage-aware and item-level rules differ by $-0.0002$ and $-0.0001$ on average, with standard deviations 0.0017 and 0.0060. The BoolQ diagonal moves by 0.03 percent and 0.15 percent. The two splitting rules therefore agree on this benchmark within their own spread.

A simulation matched to the observed passage-size histogram adds a run-by-passage interaction shared by the questions on a passage, using 500 replicates at each of five interaction scales, with standard deviation from zero up to the item-noise scale. Across those scales the passage-level and item-level splits differ in $\Lambda$ by between $-0.0008$ and $0.0022$ on average, within Monte Carlo error of zero. The observed histogram puts about 240 same-passage question pairs across the halves out of about 2.7 million cross-half pairs. At that scale a leaked interaction can't move the diagonal by more than about 0.01 percent. The null result above is therefore what the passage structure of this benchmark implies rather than evidence of a sensitive test. Outside BoolQ, the request files show two question stems shared across traits and repeated question stems within benchmarks, for example 62 of 1,838 PIQA items. We haven't grouped those repeats in our analysis.

N2 was proposed as an estimator-bias check rather than the primary inferential procedure. Our cross-format diagnostic retains the diagonal sum and only those off-diagonal terms whose traits have different formats. It has a null reference of one when those retained covariances vanish. However, the masked sum needn't represent the variance of a realisable benchmark average, and because each benchmark has only one format, the comparison can't identify a causal effect of format.

Our separate calculation reproduces the full estimate to four decimal places before retaining 54 of the 90 ordered off-diagonal pairs. We find both diagnostics below the proposed 1.2 threshold, at 0.921 with interval 0.801 to 1.035 for margins and 0.965 with interval 0.848 to 1.063 for accuracy. The margin result falls below the 1.153 expected from uniformly distributed covariance contributions under the comparison used here.

BoolQ is the only yes/no benchmark, and all of its off-diagonal pairs therefore cross a format boundary. Its margin seed variance is $1.43\times10^{-3}$, compared with $4.34\times10^{-4}$ for the next-largest trait. Excluding BoolQ gives a cross-format margin diagnostic of 1.006 with interval 0.972 to 1.039, against an unrestricted nine-trait estimate of 1.786 with interval 1.689 to 1.877.

Among the nine traits with defined margin correlations, excluding WinoGrande, the mean correlation is 0.624 across sixteen within-format pairs and 0.007 across twenty cross-format pairs. The three cloze traits give margin inflation of 1.225 with interval 1.064 to 1.367, and dropping ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge from the multiple-choice block leaves inflation of 1.479 with interval 1.416 to 1.541. We observe concentration within the larger format groups, while benchmark content and format remain confounded, and a rank-one model with trait-specific loadings can also produce uneven contributions across those groups.

Division by $s_j$ changes only the benchmark weights and lowers margin inflation from 1.244 to 1.182. The three bounded scores lower it further to between 1.120 and 1.141. The sign score gives 1.079 and differs from the accuracy estimate of 1.078 by 0.0007 for reasons we haven't traced. Across these scores the off-diagonal sum falls from 0.547 to 0.164 times the trace, BoolQ's share of that trace grows from 0.679 to 0.844, and bounded margins from the same runs reproduce between 62 and 75 percent of the gap between margin and accuracy inflation. These transformations change the scoring rule and leave the trained models untouched. They don't show how training produces large margins, and our intervals treat each $s_j$ as fixed.

\suptab{tab:original8} applies $\bar r_E=0.0181$ and holds trait standard deviations fixed, with flip probabilities interpreted under the stated Gaussian comparison model. The held-out accuracy point errors favour the full matrix over independence, 0.0105 versus 0.0143, without an interval for their difference. Every predictor also receives held-out seed standard deviations unavailable without replication. These results therefore don't establish an operational replacement for replicated runs. The three-unit PolyPythias accuracy estimate of 2.286 differs from 1.078 and has a configuration-bootstrap interval with no defined lower endpoint, and that further limits transport of this calculation.

Negative estimated variances leave eighteen margin and 34 accuracy ordered off-diagonal correlations undefined. Our implementation fills these entries with zero before differencing, including undefined diagonal entries compared with unit diagonals in $R_P$. Those diagonal substitutions contribute 1.0 and 2.0 to the squared distances.

units.new_text: For each of the 125 configurations, we selected the largest checkpoint step released for all three runs. Our analysis record describes a supplement that omits the fetch stage's complete configuration table. DataDecide stops the two auxiliary runs below 1B at 25 percent of the 1B compute budget, and it trains three complete runs only at 1B \citep{magnusson2025}. The per-instance release contains auxiliary runs from 150M upward, and our replicated sizes begin at 150M rather than 4M.

We indexed the 25 released recipe archives, and that index reproduces the selected step recorded for all 375 runs. At 530M the selected step averages 86.7 percent of the default run's final step, with configuration values from 38.9 to 88.7 percent. At 750M the same step averages 41.5 percent, with configuration values from 17.7 to 44.0 percent. The three runs reach different maximum steps in 92 of the configurations. In 26 of them, one at 530M and 25 at 750M, the largest maximum step exceeds the smallest by more than a factor of 1.5. Only 33 configurations share a final step, and 24 of those sit at 1B.

Table~\ref{tab:truncation} recomputes our two estimates on subsets defined by the index. The full sample gives margin inflation of 1.244 with interval 1.143 to 1.338 and accuracy inflation of 1.078 with interval 0.993 to 1.157. Excluding the 26 severely truncated configurations gives 1.276 with interval 1.114 to 1.420 and 1.120 for accuracy. Neither of those two wild intervals includes one. The 92 configurations with different final steps give 1.330 with interval 1.024 to 1.583 and 1.070 with interval 0.956 to 1.171. Intervals for the 33 configurations that share a final step are too wide to separate inflation from one, and 18 of their 24 recipes contribute only a 1B configuration. A configuration's influence, $(T_c-\widehat\Lam^2U_c)/\sum_{c'}U_{c'}$, has Spearman correlation $-0.036$ for margins and $0.001$ for accuracy with the selected step's share of the default final step. Permuting that share within each size over 4,999 draws gives $p=0.314$ and $p=0.990$. We chose these subsets after seeing the full-sample estimates, so they describe sensitivity rather than testing a hypothesis, and Table~\ref{tab:original7} gives estimates by size as a further check.

Our realised standard errors are smaller by factors of 2.1 and 3.3, against a factor of approximately 1.21 that the larger configuration count alone would predict. Interpolating the N1 simulation grid gives dispersion at the planned $\bar r_E=0.0911$. That dispersion is 1.04 times the dispersion at the observed margin value of 0.061 and 1.13 times the dispersion at the accuracy value of 0.0181. The design effect at $\rho_{\mathrm{ICC}}=0.15$ and the reliability also differ, but we haven't separated their contributions. The planned accuracy MDE is 1.412, with a separate power entry at $\bar r_E=0.115$. We retain our original planning calculations rather than calculating power from the estimated effect after observing the results.

The planning document lists nine checks with proposed responses, and its claimed date of September 5, 2026 lacks an independent timestamp. We treat it as a reported plan and its checks as exploratory assessments.

A batch offset can enter the same cross-trait products as run-level variation, and our auxiliary-run contrast removes it. The three-run estimate stays exposed to that offset. The batch-offset null N6 adds a shared default-versus-auxiliary offset with standard deviation 0.05 to the zero-correlation population. It gives mean factors of 1.004 on margins and 1.003 on accuracy over 2,000 replicates, with 1.000 on both scales under the auxiliary-run contrast. Check G8 passes on point estimates, with an auxiliary-run margin of 1.256 against the gate's threshold of 1.122, one plus half the full-battery excess of 0.244. However, the intervals cross the decision boundaries and the full-set estimate stays uncorrected for this exposure.

Under the default gain simulator, $\sigma_g=0.05$ produces approximately 61 percent of the observed margin excess, and an empirically matched simulator produces approximately eight percent at the same gain scale and six percent at the estimated scale of 0.042. We read these results as sensitivity to simulator assumptions rather than as causal bounds on the contribution of gain. The accuracy result offers no independent protection because multiplying a margin by a positive factor leaves its sign unchanged. \suptab{tab:original5} records every planning check beside its recorded outcome. Those outcomes include the 125 parsed cells at G0, power of 1.00 against an inflation of 1.427 at $\rho_g=0.73$ for G1, a median information ratio of 1.61 at G2, and an offset of at most 0.002 at G4.

Our target adds covariance between benchmark-specific run deviations. \citet{jordan2024} compares shifted versions of one benchmark, and \citet{bui2025} and \citet{hochlehnert2025} vary fine-tuning and decoding seeds, a source of variation distinct from pretraining-run variation. \citet[Section 4.3]{dodge2020} compare four GLUE task rankings across seeds without a covariance matrix. \citet{cheverud2001}, \citet{nyholt2004}, and \citet{li2005} count effective independent tests to adjust significance thresholds, and we instead convert a noise covariance into an effective benchmark count. \citet{searle1992} explain negative moment estimates when the true component lies near zero. \citet{schaeffer2023} show how discontinuous metrics change apparent trends, and accuracy thresholds our margin at zero, and we therefore report both scales, although low seed signal relative to item noise limits accuracy here. \citet{dehghani2021}, \citet{demsar2006}, \citet{dror2017}, \citet{card2020}, \citet{gorman2019}, and \citet{burnell2023} address benchmark selection, inference, power, split dependence, and per-instance reporting. \citet{henderson2018} and \citet{agarwal2021} resample runs within tasks, and our analysis must preserve paired run effects across benchmarks instead. \citet{hardy2026}, \citet{kohli2026}, \citet{messing2026}, and \citet{sha2026} measure dependence across models, judges, or prompts. We measure paired deviations across training runs instead.

\paragraph{Covariance diagnostics}
We put the largest discrepancy between opposite cross-half covariance entries at 2.44 bootstrap standard errors, and that gap doesn't by itself establish leakage. The reduced item records provide 57 MMLU subject groups but only one group for each other trait. Our passage-aware split in Appendix~\ref{app:derivations} uses the release's request files instead.

Among the eight accuracy traits with positive estimated seed variance, estimated correlations range from $-0.216$ to 1.296. The symmetrised matrix has a negative eigenvalue of $-0.55$. These estimates don't form a valid correlation matrix, a possible finite-sample outcome of noise-corrected moment estimation. We retain the unprojected matrix because a positive-semidefinite projection would change the reported values without an established correction target, and our primary ratio uses cross-half sums directly. The nine-trait margin matrix has nine positive eigenvalues, though the indefinite accuracy matrix yields no validated count of independent population directions.

The lower squared-ratio bound for 1B margins falls below zero, which leaves its square-root endpoint unavailable. The cluster-robust $t(24)$ interval on the log of the squared ratio gives 0.811 to 1.628, the configuration percentile bootstrap gives 0.834 to 1.643, and the wild bootstrap on the log of the squared ratio gives 0.491 to 1.656. Three positive constructions give finite endpoints, and none of them excludes one.

That same run also estimated every size band with BoolQ removed. On margins the bands give 1.548, 1.864, 1.874, 1.888 and 1.649 from 150M to 1B, with intervals of \ci{1.325}{1.742}, \ci{1.763}{1.961}, \ci{1.694}{2.039}, \ci{1.660}{2.082} and \ci{1.215}{2.001}. Every band then excludes one, and our 1B cell recovers a finite lower endpoint. On accuracy the same removal gives 1.842, 1.900, 1.548, 1.594 and 1.222, with intervals of \ci{0.989}{2.408}, \ci{1.174}{2.417}, \ci{1.262}{1.792}, \ci{1.341}{1.811} and \ci{0.429}{1.674}. We scored those constructions in a separate run inside one size band at the three runs the release ships, and our transform doesn't repair that case. On an accuracy-like band the log interval misses in 0.151 of replicates against 0.017 for the plain one, and it therefore buys definedness on that band by paying coverage. At the full 125-cell design the two constructions agree within 0.006 across the dependence structures we simulated, and both fail together near 0.82 at a band-shared quarter. The leverage correction alone improves on either, holding 0.954 at the joint corner. In a thin cell the transform keeps endpoints positive without giving a better interval (seed 20260978, 4,000 replicates).

Simulation says these per-size rows should be read as estimates with wide uncertainty rather than as intervals carrying their nominal level. The accuracy column is the weaker of the two. One band at three runs covers 0.930 on a margin-like population and only 0.707 on an accuracy-like one, and ten runs lift the accuracy case to 0.947. Power inside a single band is worse again. An additional exploratory baseline, P2R, rescales $R_P$ off-diagonals by the training-fold ratio of mean noise correlation to mean performance correlation. Its mean factors are 0.366 for margins and 0.370 for accuracy, against whole-population ratios of 0.375 and 0.362, and on the same five recipe folds its squared prediction errors are 0.0131 and 0.0342. P2R improves on P2 and still runs 2.3 times worse than P1 on margins, and worse than independence on accuracy. Its direction relative to independence holds on margins in all 1,000 random fold partitions and on accuracy in 987 of them. Yet the recipe-bootstrap intervals below include zero on both scales. This rescaling also requires replicated runs to estimate its factor.

\paragraph{Paired uncertainty for the prediction comparison}\label{app:paired}
Table~\ref{tab:prediction} gives the fold-mean prediction errors that Section~\ref{sec:prediction} summarises for each of the six models. Each model receives the held-out marginal seed standard deviations, which isolates the correlation component. We find a margin gain and no accuracy gain. On margins the rank-one, rank-one plus gain, and full models each lower the mean squared error of log aggregate standard deviation by about 0.03 from the 0.0358 of independence, with paired recipe-bootstrap intervals that exclude zero. The rank-one interval reaches zero when nonpositive held-out variances are filled from training folds, and on accuracy every interval for a difference from independence includes zero. The unrescaled phenotypic plug-in has the largest error on both scales. In an operational comparison that refits every matrix without held-out marginals and predicts each held-out configuration's raw variance moment, no model separates from independence. Before fitting any model we clip negative variance estimates, while the target retains the original covariance contributions.

The rank-one model has the lowest margin point error and full covariance the lowest accuracy point error. Trait removal changes our estimates more than recipe or size removal. Exclusion of BoolQ gives 1.786 with interval 1.689 to 1.877 for margins, and 1.558 with interval 1.412 to 1.687 for accuracy. Exclusion of CommonsenseQA gives the smallest point estimates, 1.096 and 1.014. WinoGrande is the only other removal whose accuracy interval, 1.023 to 1.178, excludes one. The table gives the remaining intervals and standard deviations. BoolQ contributes 68 percent of the estimated margin variance trace and 84 percent of the accuracy trace. The removal estimates imply that the off-diagonal terms involving BoolQ are negative, summing to about $-0.15$ of the margin trace and $-0.06$ of the accuracy trace. Its removal lowers the denominator by more than the numerator. The same removal also lowers the aggregate standard deviation on both scales, as \suptab{tab:original10} shows. A larger inflation factor therefore accompanies a less variable average.

We also lowered BoolQ's weight below the flat tenth in seven steps to 0.0533, raising the other nine weights together so the battery still sums to one. Margin inflation climbs from 1.2439 at the flat weighting to 1.5030 at the smallest weight, and every interval along the way excludes one. Accuracy climbs from 1.0784 to 1.2311 over the same steps. Its interval stops including one at a BoolQ weight of 0.0867, a reduction of about one seventh. Because the estimate moves smoothly, the accuracy conclusion is a knife edge in the weighting, since a battery that discounts BoolQ by a seventh reports dependence on accuracy as well. We report the flat weighting because the release gives no basis for singling out BoolQ, and the item-count weighting below is the one alternative its own counts supply. A reader with such a basis should expect the accuracy answer to move first.

Standardisation of traits by estimated seed standard deviation gives 1.803 on nine margin traits and 1.707 on eight accuracy traits. These point diagnostics omit traits with nonpositive variance estimates and divide by uncertain standard deviations, with seven accuracy traits at or below item noise. With those estimated weights held fixed, the wild recipe-cluster intervals are 1.544 to 2.023 and 1.228 to 2.076. They omit the uncertainty in the weights themselves, and we don't score them against the planning thresholds. Removal of defined traits from the standardised batteries gives margin estimates from 1.625 to 1.910 and accuracy estimates from 1.388 to 1.780. Selection of traits by positive estimated variance can change the target. It could raise the mean correlation if the excluded low-signal traits also have low true correlations, which is an assumption we haven't tested.

Our trait-removal spans are descriptive composition diagnostics, because the ten fixed benchmarks aren't established exchangeable draws from a benchmark population. The raw spans are 0.690 for margins and 0.544 for accuracy, against interval widths of 0.195 and 0.164. The delete-one-trait jackknife formula gives scales of 0.554 and 0.455. The matching sampling standard errors are 0.045 and 0.038, and without the BoolQ removal value those scales fall to 0.139 and 0.073. A normal calculation on the jackknife scales and sampling standard errors added in quadrature gives ranges of 0.15 to 2.33 and 0.18 to 1.974, both including one. Without the BoolQ value the same arithmetic gives 0.958 to 1.529 and 0.918 to 1.239. Those ranges aren't validated confidence intervals, since they can double-count sampling variation and the normal approximation behaves poorly near the parameter boundary, where $\Lambda=0.15$ corresponds to $\bar r_E=-0.109$, only about 0.003 above $-1/9$. We retain the fixed-battery target and report composition sensitivity without treating these scales as an identified decomposition of total uncertainty.

A change in trait count also changes $\Lambda$ at fixed effective covariance coefficient. At $\bar r_E=0.061$, the nine-trait reference is 1.219 rather than the ten-trait 1.244. The corresponding accuracy values are 1.070 and 1.078, and four margin removals and five accuracy removals exceed those mechanical references. On eight traits, standardised accuracy inflation of 1.707 implies 2.75 effective benchmarks, while the raw accuracy effective coefficient of 0.0181 implies 7.10 effective benchmarks. The comparison of 2.75 with 7.10 holds trait count fixed, unlike comparison with the ten-trait value of 8.60.

At fixed benchmark count, subsets that contain BoolQ have mean margin inflation lower by 0.115 at two benchmarks and by 0.596 at nine. The corresponding accuracy differences are 0.076 and 0.499. units.new_text: A separate implementation of our interval definitions gives empirical coverage from 0.920 to 0.975 across sixteen cells of 200 datasets. The four cells with dispersion 0.044, close to the observed null dispersions of 0.046 and 0.048, cover 0.950, 0.935, 0.975, and 0.960. This limited simulation doesn't validate all departures present in the study.

A second simulation with 2,000 replicates per population and 4,999 draws scores four interval procedures on the same simulated moments. Table~\ref{tab:coverage} lists the populations, each with 125 configurations in 25 recipe clusters, three runs, and ten benchmarks. We find that the wild bootstrap-$t$ covers between 0.928 and 0.954. The cluster $t(24)$ tracks it within 0.02 but falls to 0.911 with one recipe at six times the variance. The configuration percentile bootstrap falls to 0.872 under recipe-shared run effects, while the recipe percentile bootstrap covers between 0.857 and 0.940 with undefined draws in the accuracy-like noise cells. Cross-half error correlation of 0.1 biases the estimate by $-0.014$ and $-0.016$, and its margin-like wild interval misses above in 0.066 of replicates against a nominal 0.025. That shortfall therefore falls on one side rather than on both. The accuracy-like population with mean correlation 0.018 carries a bias of $-0.007$.

We later added a centred cluster test-inversion interval, whose accepted set can be unbounded. It is bounded in 23,999 of the same 24,000 simulated datasets. It covers between 0.932 and 0.957 and holds 0.955 with one recipe at six times the variance, where the wild interval gives 0.930. A restricted variant without centring covers between 0.946 and 0.970, above 0.95 in eleven of the twelve populations. A repeat of all twelve populations at 10,000 replicates puts the centred inversion between 0.935 and 0.956 and the wild interval between 0.933 and 0.953.

The Monte Carlo standard error of 0.005 is the size of the shortfalls in Table~\ref{tab:coverage}. We repeated every cell at 10,000 replicates with new seeds, and no cell moves by more than 0.011 under that repeat. In the four cells that matter most, our wild interval covers 0.933 with cross-half correlation 0.1, 0.935 with one dominant recipe, 0.940 in the margin-like cell, and 0.945 in the accuracy-like cell. A third seed moves the margin-like cell to 0.951 before it settles at 0.946 over 60,000 pooled replicates, while the other three repeat within 0.004. The centred inversion covers 0.935, 0.956, 0.942, and 0.947 in the same four cells, where it keeps its advantage of 0.021 under one dominant recipe while matching the wild interval elsewhere. A further sweep with a third seed puts the wild interval between 0.929 and 0.950 across all twelve. We conclude that the shortfall belongs to the construction rather than to one set of draws.

We then applied all eight of our constructions to the data itself with 9,999 draws over twenty bootstrap seeds. On the full battery the margin interval runs from 1.141 to 1.339 under Rademacher weights, 1.130 to 1.349 under residual scaling, and 1.095 to 1.323 under the centred inversion. All eight exclude one on margins and include one on accuracy. Removal of BoolQ leaves both scales above one under all eight, where the widest margin interval is the restricted inversion at 1.391 to 1.840. A separate simulation scored an independent population at one in ten, one in twenty and one in a hundred, giving 0.896, 0.951 and 0.990, so the interval tracks the level it claims. A band-shared quarter breaks all three levels together, at 0.743, 0.828 and 0.928.

We compared six further constructions on the same twelve populations. A wild bootstrap-$t$ whose recipe residual is divided by $1-h_g$, with $h_g$ the recipe's share of the denominator sum, covers between 0.943 and 0.958 at 4,000 replicates. Our shipped version covers 0.932 to 0.951 there. At 10,000 replicates it improves every cell by between 0.007 and 0.014, reaches 0.95 in ten cells where the shipped version reaches it in one, and runs 4 to 13 percent wider at the median. We picked it after seeing the first four cells. The eight that followed confirm it on the same generator family rather than test it independently, and we report the shipped interval throughout. On the observed data it gives \ci{1.130}{1.349} for margins and \ci{0.987}{1.163} for accuracy, which moves no conclusion but erases the 0.011 of separation from the planned threshold that we report below.

Prepivoting measures calibration inside the resampling model that our interval already assumes, and a violation the bootstrap shares with the estimator stays invisible to it. Beran prepivoting, a second wild bootstrap of 1,999 draws inside each of 1,999 outer resamples, calibrates the full-battery margin interval to \ci{1.151}{1.328}. That interval runs 0.018 narrower than the shipped \ci{1.143}{1.338} and still excludes one. Accuracy calibrates to \ci{0.994}{1.161} and still includes one, and the BoolQ-removed margin interval calibrates to \ci{1.689}{1.878}. In the four simulated cells that carry the shortfall it gives 0.924, 0.933, 0.931 and 0.944 against 0.938, 0.931, 0.936 and 0.953 for the shipped interval. We find that prepivoting repairs none of the shortfall.

Our estimator assumes that item noise in one half doesn't correlate with item noise in the other. We swept the cross-half noise correlation from $-0.1$ to 0.5 with 1,000 replicates at each value. The mean margin estimate stays between 0.997 and 1.001 and no margin replicate reaches the observed 1.244, because such noise pulls a real inflation toward one. On accuracy the null dispersion is wide enough that 0.19 of replicates reach the observed 1.078 with no correlation at all.

A scalar effect shared across benchmarks and repeated across halves is a different matter, because the numerator absorbs all of it and the denominator only a tenth. We swept its share of item-noise variance with 2,000 replicates at each value. A share near 0.124 reproduces the observed 1.244, and at a share of 0.05 only 0.007 of replicates reach the observed value. Small amounts of this contamination therefore don't explain the margin result. Accuracy is far more fragile, because the same construction reaches the observed 1.078 at a share near 0.009. We haven't measured this component in the released scores. Because a regression diagnostic can't separate it from a seed covariance that follows the item-noise scales, that check has no power.

A permutation of run deviations across the items of one group, separately for every run, breaks only the tie between particular items and particular runs. Over 2,000 permutations of the 37,682 items in their 66 groups, 0.087 of the permutations reach or exceed the observed margin 1.244, and 0.352 reach or exceed the observed accuracy. The item-level channel therefore accounts for about 0.001 of the margin estimate and 0.002 of the accuracy estimate, against excesses over one of 0.244 and 0.078. Re-drawing the item half split 200 times in that kernel, separately from the fifty re-splits of the primary run, gives a margin range of 1.242 to 1.254 and an accuracy median of 1.083 with a range of 1.059 to 1.103. We observe that the shipped 1.244 and 1.078 aren't a favourable draw. The real re-split standard deviations of 0.0018 and 0.0083 exceed the permuted values of 0.0009 and 0.0053. Item-level structure does survive and widens the spread without moving the centre. However, an effect that every item of a benchmark carries survives this permutation untouched, and only the sub-benchmark form of the violation is bounded here.

\paragraph{Observed gaps and predicted rank reversals}
Our Gaussian calculation puts many same-size pairs inside the reversal-prone range. With accuracy noise $\sigma_{\rm agg}=0.00514$, it gives $P_{\rm flip}>0.05$ for a true gap below 0.01196, and 455 of the $5\binom{25}{2}=1{,}500$ observed same-size pairs fall below it. We find that a plug-in correction restores nominal size where the uncorrected rule doesn't. We simulated a practitioner's correction under three-run noise, over 4,000 replicates that build our shipped design and estimate the ratio from it. Each replicate then tests a fresh comparison under an uncorrected rule, a plug-in rule scaled by the estimate, and an oracle rule with the true value. At a true margin gap of zero the rules declare in 0.113, 0.051 and 0.050 of replicates against a nominal 0.05, and three runs per model leave those at 0.115, 0.053 and 0.051. The plug-in rule sits within 0.005 of the oracle in every cell despite the estimate's noise. An accuracy-like population gives 0.067, 0.052 and 0.047.

Extra runs buy nothing against the size error, because both standard errors fall with the square root of the run count. Our sweeps to ten, 80 and 360 runs per model show this directly. Across one to ten runs the uncorrected rule declares at a zero margin gap in 0.112 to 0.122 of replicates against 0.047 to 0.056 corrected, and accuracy gives 0.061 to 0.078 against 0.047 to 0.063. Runs buy power instead, from 0.100 of replicates at one run to 0.614 at ten for a margin gap of one aggregate standard deviation, or 0.111 to 0.615 on accuracy. We observe substantial checkpoint sensitivity in this restricted sample. Our design can't fully separate stochastic trajectory variation from systematic progress across 1,000 steps.

Our estimator describes run variation at the scored checkpoint, which can include trajectory effects correlated across traits. It doesn't isolate initialisation from these effects in the available design. This comparison uses 1,800 rather than 4,755 items, nine runs, and a final checkpoint, whereas DataDecide uses common steps during training. Both are fitted to the same data that the intervals describe.

We find that the two interval families agree at the top and part at the bottom. On the observed data the centred inversion gives 1.095 to 1.323 for margins and 0.995 to 1.162 for accuracy, beside wild intervals of 1.143 to 1.338 and 0.993 to 1.157. The upper endpoints differ by at most 0.015, but the inversion puts the margin lower endpoint 0.048 lower. The wild lower endpoint shouldn't be read as a firm floor. In the size bands the inversion gives 0.765 to 1.737 for 530M margins and 1.024 to 1.398 for 530M accuracy. That margin interval includes one although the wild interval excludes it. The accuracy interval in that band still excludes one. The accuracy intervals after BoolQ and WinoGrande removal stay above one at 1.397 to 1.716 and 1.026 to 1.184.

The analysis also reports 1,000 trait-specific run-label permutations, each using 4,999 bootstrap draws, whose intervals contain the reference value one in 0.925 of margin permutations and 0.954 of accuracy permutations. Our repeat with 2,000 permutations gives 0.944 on margins and 0.949 on accuracy. Ten further runs at 1,000 permutations put margin coverage between 0.915 and 0.942. Thus the reported record reads as one coarse draw. The margin interval falls below the null in 0.032 to 0.052 of permutations against a nominal 0.025. That lower-tail imbalance matters for an upper bound below the proposed threshold of 1.349, where the reported upper endpoint leaves only 0.011 of separation.

These are conditional randomisation results, contingent on the exchangeability assumed by the permutations, and they aren't coverage measurements for the unknown nonzero covariance of the original population. The cluster-$t$ comparator has recorded coverage of 0.881 and 0.941 against our repeat's 0.901 and 0.938. The accuracy upper-tail fraction is 0.021 in the record and 0.020 in the repeat. That figure is close to the 0.028 of the earlier 500 draws.

The Mistral release of \citet{karamcheti2021} provides five GPT-2 Small and five GPT-2 Medium runs with about 600 checkpoints each, listed as 610 in the release summary, including WikiText-103 and OpenWebText validation perplexity. However, the source search didn't find the corresponding per-run benchmark battery. Without paired held-out loss and benchmark scores from the same runs, we can't use that release to identify the gain contribution.

Our pooled in-sample fit over the 250 run contrasts gives margin and accuracy inflation of 1.275 and 1.097 after gain adjustment, 1.276 and 1.094 after gain and competence together, and 1.244 and 1.076 after competence alone. The repair we fixed before seeing its output standardises by seed variances shrunk halfway toward their median positive value, cross-fitted over recipe folds. It gives margin inflation of 0.731 with interval 0.673 to 0.784, and accuracy inflation of 1.004 with interval 0.925 to 1.075.

Our split-half check shows that the shipped proxy carries no measurable signal about the run it scores, since its half-A and half-B scores correlate at $-0.086$ on margins and $-0.072$ on accuracy. For this revision we fitted four proxy weightings out of fold, and a one-factor proxy with regression-score weights reaches 0.965 and 0.738 on the same check.

Our adjusted margin estimate stops separating from independence. Cross-fitted margin inflation is 1.245 under the shipped weighting, 0.731 after shrinkage, 0.973 for the factor proxy, and 0.889 when the clipped benchmarks are dropped. A 999-draw recipe bootstrap that refits the whole pipeline gives 0.935 to 1.018 for the factor proxy on margins and 0.970 to 1.104 on accuracy. None of the four manufactures covariance where none exists. Under simulated independent seed deviations they all return a mean between 0.998 and 1.003. None of this identifies mediation either, because every one of these proxies averages the same seed deviations that it adjusts and so removes shared covariance by construction. With the observed seed covariance and no competence variable at all, the four weightings return margin means of 1.097, 0.745, 0.980, and 1.029, and the observed cross-fitted values sit inside the central 90 percent of those simulations for the shipped, shrunk, and factor weightings on both scales. None of them carries evidence of a competence mechanism beyond covariance removal. Those simulations refit the cross-fitted pipeline in every replicate, and their percentiles therefore describe a different estimator from the in-sample matched means in Table~\ref{tab:proxy}. The clipped-drop weighting is the one departure, since its observed cross-fitted 0.889 on margins and 0.994 on accuracy fall below simulated fifth percentiles of 0.908 and 1.003. Under a common correlation of 0.178 the factor weighting returns 0.852 on margins, so these proxies can overshoot under equicorrelation.

On excess inflation the DataDecide prediction falls approximately 40 percent below PolyPythias. The raw inflation difference is approximately twelve percent and falls inside the proposed twenty-percent band. However, the planning document names aggregate standard deviation without resolving this scale choice, and that leaves our excess-based failure assessment post hoc.

An exploratory extension adds the 14M and 31M configurations with nine runs each at step 143000. Within that rescore margin inflation changes from 1.41372 at three sizes to 1.26199 at five sizes, with the excess ratio moving from 1.69592 to 1.07393. The configuration-bootstrap interval for five-size accuracy runs from 0.869 to 2.428. At three sizes its lower endpoint is undefined, with an upper endpoint of 2.971. We find margin intervals of 0.939 to 1.781 at three sizes and 0.927 to 1.537 at five sizes, and both contain one and DataDecide's 1.24395. Since the bootstrap resamples only three or five configurations, we also inverted the centred cluster test described above with each configuration as its own cluster. That inversion gives margin sets of 0 to 2.106 at three sizes and 0.519 to 1.664 at five sizes. It can't exclude any nonnegative accuracy value, and these data therefore don't bound PolyPythias accuracy inflation.

Our repeat on two T4 GPUs reproduces every reported estimate, interval, and standard error, with the same scorer, token cap, items, and checkpoints. The rescore itself used one T4 with a 6,000-token cap instead of 30,000 tokens, and its three-size margin value of 1.41372 differs from the pipeline's 1.40574 by 0.6 percent. Against a single configuration's ratio our decomposition doesn't show out-of-sample value. Nine seeds per configuration let us ask whether a three-run fit predicts the measured ratio. That ratio is the standard deviation of the battery mean divided by the root of the weighted sum of per-benchmark variances, item noise included. For each of the 84 ways of choosing three runs, we predicted it on the six runs left out, where independence predicts one, the plug-in predicts the inflation estimate, and our decomposition adds each benchmark's estimated item noise to both sides. On margins across three sizes the mean absolute log error is 0.339 for independence, 0.536 for the plug-in, and 0.512 for the decomposition. For a recipe subset $S$, the estimator is $\widehat\Lambda_S=\sqrt{\sum_{c\in S}T_c/\sum_{c\in S}U_c}$. The margin interval keeps excluding one under every recipe, pair and benchmark deletion. The one exception is the 530M band, whose removal leaves 1.178 with an interval of 0.993 to 1.338, a lower endpoint 0.007 below one. Simulation puts at least one band-deletion failure in 0.164 of populations whose full interval excludes one. One failure out of five is therefore close to chance. We find our accuracy conclusion fragile in the opposite direction. Its full-battery interval includes one yet stops including it under five of the 25 recipe deletions, under removal of the 750M band, and under removal of WinoGrande or BoolQ. All eight exceptions put the whole interval above one, with the BoolQ removal's lower endpoint at 1.412. Among simulated null populations with a true ratio of one whose full interval includes one, five or more recipe deletions flip in 0.018, and a second null calibrated to the observed 1.078 puts that at 0.032. The observed five flips therefore sit in the upper few percent of what a deletion sweep produces by chance, and all move towards more inflation.

With clusters on the five size bands instead of the 25 recipes, the margin interval runs from 1.030 to 1.426 and still excludes one, while the matching accuracy interval runs from 0.961 to 1.184 and still includes one. The two-way clustered variance turns negative on full-battery margins and returns an implausibly small accuracy standard error, and we therefore report neither. units.new_text: Our pipeline streams 122.9 GB of gzipped JSONL tarballs from the Hugging Face release, and it retains the item identifier, correct-answer margin, and accuracy bit for the ten traits at the common checkpoint. Each run contains 37,682 items and approximately 30 MB of compressed output, and reducing the 375 runs produces approximately 48 MB of NumPy archives, one array per run.

A frozen master seed generates a balanced permutation of item order within each trait, and our split uses that permutation rather than a hash of item identifiers. All runs within an arm reuse the same trait-specific assignment, which gives the PolyPythias subsample its own split rather than an item-hash split shared across arms. Regenerating it requires the recorded item ordering and randomisation specification, without downloading the full tarballs.
We compute every derived quantity in the paper from unrounded estimates, and recomputation from the printed three-decimal values can therefore differ in the final digit.

We state the source calculation in terms of the squared ratio,
\[
\widehat\theta=\frac{\sum_cT_c}{\sum_cU_c},\qquad
\widehat\Lambda=\sqrt{\widehat\theta}. \]
For each recipe $g$ among $G=25$, the linearised contribution and standard error in Equation~\ref{eq:bootstrap} are
\begin{equation}
\psi_g=\frac{\sum_{c\in g}(T_c-\widehat\theta U_c)}{\sum_cU_c},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=\left(\sum_{g=1}^{G}\psi_g^2\right)^{1/2}. \label{eq:bootstrap}
\end{equation}
This standard error belongs to the squared-ratio scale used for studentisation. A reported standard error on the $\Lambda$ scale instead requires the corresponding delta-method conversion.

For draw $b$, independent recipe signs satisfy $v_{bg}\in\{-1,+1\}$ with equal probabilities, every configuration takes the sign assigned to its recipe, and the pseudo-numerator becomes \[ T_c^*=\widehat\theta U_c+v_{bg(c)}(T_c-\widehat\theta U_c). \]
The denominator remains fixed at the observed $\sum_cU_c$, and we recompute $\widehat\theta_b^*=\sum_cT_c^*/\sum_cU_c$ and the bootstrap standard error from the residuals $T_c^*-\widehat\theta_b^*U_c$. The bootstrap statistic is $t_b^*=(\widehat\theta_b^*-\widehat\theta)/\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_b^*$, and our source calculation uses 4,999 draws with bootstrap seed zero. Our CPU kernels carried the estimation, bootstrap, and permutation work on Python 3.12.13 with NumPy 2.0.2 under Linux, while the scoring and calibration kernels ran on GPU cards. The draws come from NumPy's default generator, whose stream is tied to that version.

Writing $q_\alpha$ for the empirical quantile of these statistics, the interval on $\theta$ is
\[
\left[\widehat\theta-q_{0.975}\widehat{\mathrm{SE}},
\widehat\theta-q_{0.025}\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}\right]. \]
Square-root transformation gives endpoints on the inflation scale when both endpoints are nonnegative. Monotonicity preserves the ordering of available endpoints, but it doesn't establish the original interval's coverage.

A draw with zero bootstrap standard error has no finite studentised statistic, and our routine discards it. The routine requires at least $\max(100,0.9B)$ surviving draws before it reports an interval. A negative lower squared-ratio endpoint is recorded as missing rather than truncated, and that convention explains the absent 1B margin lower endpoint in Table~\ref{tab:original7}. The configuration percentile bootstrap instead resamples all 125 configurations with replacement, recomputes both sums, and ignores recipe membership.

Our planning document specified wild cluster bootstrap-t inference with $t(16)$ critical values for seventeen estimation recipes. Our realised analysis instead uses empirical bootstrap quantiles over all 25 recipes, because we failed to implement the planned split. The analysis record states that a $t(G-1)$ variant accompanies the bootstrap implementation. These alternatives differ in more than a change of cluster count.

Within-configuration centring removes the shared performance mean before we form cross-half products, since with only three runs the raw products would include a large contribution from mean competence rather than measuring covariance of deviations. Our contrast representation in Appendix~\ref{app:centring} enforces that centring at the estimator input.

Our permutation procedure reassigns run labels independently within each trait, and applying one joint permutation to all traits instead preserves cross-trait pairing and therefore doesn't generate this independence null. Identity permutations remain valid members of the randomisation distribution and shouldn't be excluded. For three runs, independent identities across all $K$ traits have probability $6^{-K}$ within one configuration.
